claims.text: Chemical dealloying can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks from noble metal-based high-entropy alloy precursors.
Electrochemical dealloying can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks from noble metal-based high-entropy alloy precursors.
Dealloying preferentially removes the more active, less-noble constituents of the precursor.
Selective removal of less-noble constituents leaves a porous, interconnected noble-metal network.
The porous, interconnected noble-metal network is beneficial for catalysis.
The proposed precursor contains both noble and less-noble components in a high-entropy, near-equiatomic configuration.
An acidic or alkaline electrolyte can provide an environment for selective dissolution when the constituent elements differ sufficiently in electrochemical nobility.
Optimizing concentration, temperature, potential, and treatment time can yield a uniform porous structure.
Localized removal of reactive elements creates nanoscale ligaments and pores.
The resulting nanoscale ligaments and pores self-organize into a connected three-dimensional framework.
Differential electrochemical reactivity causes less-stable alloy constituents to dissolve selectively while noble constituents remain.
The retained noble elements reorganize to form a high-surface-area three-dimensional nanoframework.
The three-dimensional nanoframework exposes active catalytic sites.
Dealloying will produce a porous high-entropy alloy with an interconnected noble-metal network.
The dealloyed material will exhibit enhanced catalytic activity because of increased accessible surface area and complex surface structures.
The undealloyed bulk high-entropy alloy has lower surface area than the proposed dealloyed framework.
The undealloyed bulk high-entropy alloy lacks the interconnected porous morphology proposed to improve catalytic performance.
Successful framework formation requires a sufficient difference in nobility among the alloy constituents.
If constituent reactivities are too similar, dealloying may fail to produce the desired porous framework.
Precise control of pore size, ligament uniformity, and atomic-scale composition in noble metal-based high-entropy alloys requires further optimization and experimental validation.
